title: Hand, tongue, heart
hook: whoever sees a wrong, change it with the hand, then the tongue, then the heart, the weakest faith
tomorrow: he pointed at his chest three times. what was he pointing at?

segments.voice: Yesterday, proof on the claimant: the one who accuses brings the evidence. Prove it first. Today, a wrong that needs no proof, because you saw it.

A clip in the feed: someone getting mocked in a hallway, laughter all around, the phone held steady. Scrolling past is the easiest thing in the world. Yesterday's question: you see a wrong you can't fix; is doing nothing ever okay? Hadith thirty-four, in Sahih Muslim, answers with a ladder. Whoever of you sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand. If he can't, then with his tongue. If he can't, then with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith.
screen: `A CLIP IN THE FEED.` → `SCROLLING IS EASY.` → `A LADDER WITH THREE RUNGS.`

segments.voice: So the answer: doing nothing outside can be okay, when you truly can't. Doing nothing inside never is. The heart rung isn't a shrug; scholars explain it as hating the wrong and refusing to call it fine. And the ladder runs on ability, not bravado. The hand belongs to whoever can actually change the thing: a parent at home, a person in charge. The tongue is a word, said well. The Qur'an even tells Moses and Aaron to speak to Pharaoh gently. Here's the scene behind the hadith, worth telling a friend tonight: on an Eid, a governor starts the sermon before the prayer, against the custom. A man stands and objects out loud. And Abu Sa'id says: that man has done what was on him, and reports this hadith. Now, a neighbor. The Torah has a close cousin of this, read by Jews to this day. In the JPS 1917 words: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour, and not bear sin because of him." Shared ground: don't stay quiet about a wrong, and speak to win the person back, not to win. An honest difference: in Leviticus the heart is where you guard your brother, so anger doesn't settle there, and the rabbis of the Talmud add that a rebuke must never shame. In the hadith the heart is the last rung, where the wrong itself is rejected. Same door, two ways through it, ranked by no one.
screen: `HAND, THEN TONGUE, THEN HEART.` · `THE LADDER RUNS ON ABILITY.` · `A MAN OBJECTS ON EID.` · `LEVITICUS: REBUKE, DON'T HATE.` · then, large: `AT LEAST WITH THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one wrong you've seen lately and let slide. Climb the ladder honestly: is anything within my hand's reach? Is there one word I could say, gently? If neither, does my heart still call it wrong? Rest on whichever rung is true; the last one is quiet, but it isn't nothing.
screen: `ONE WRONG YOU LET SLIDE.` · `HAND? TONGUE? HEART?`

segments.voice: Hand. The first rung of the ladder: change a wrong with your hand, if it's yours to change. Then the tongue, then the heart.
Carry this: at least with the heart, and with the hand or the tongue whenever they can reach. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars teach this hadith as a duty scaled to ability: those with authority act, others speak with wisdom and gentleness, and everyone at least rejects the wrong in the heart.

fork.setup: a Jewish classmate tells you the Torah says: rebuke your neighbor, and don't hate him in your heart. same as hand, tongue, heart? what's fair to say?
options: they're the same teaching, just in different words.
both say speak up about a wrong; in Leviticus the heart guards the person, in the hadith it rejects the wrong.
they disagree: one says speak up, the other says keep it in your heart.
fork.reveal: shared ground, and an honest difference. both refuse silence about a wrong; they give the heart different jobs.

chat.says: kids keep calling Leo 'charity case' in the hall. i can't fix the whole school. so i just... don't?
options: Do what's in reach: a word to one of them, or stand next to Leo. Never call it fine.
If you can't stop all of it, nothing's on you. The heart rung means you can ignore it.
Report every one of them today. Only the hand counts; words and hearts are too weak.
chat.meaning: The ladder runs on what you can do: hand, then tongue, then heart. The heart rung is the minimum, never a shrug.
